Only `mnemonic` is merged into vocabulary.json and shipped to the browser; everything else is build-time input for scripts/generate-mnemonic-images.py. Style, aspect ratio, quality and negative prompt live in that script, never here.

_tone_glyphs.—: mid — flat, sits in the middle
_tone_glyphs.▁: low — flat, sits at the bottom

entries.mnemonic: A SWAT team smashes through the door, rifles up — then the lead officer lowers his weapon, presses his palms together and says softly, "sa-WAT-dee." The whole squad copies him. Even a raid starts with hello. (— levels out flat and calm on dee)
entries.headline: Sa-WAT-dee.
entries.scene: Four armoured SWAT officers stand in a smashed doorway, rifles lowered; the leader presses his palms together in a bowing wai greeting. Dusty Thai apartment interior, daylight flooding through the broken door.

entries.mnemonic: A market vendor holds up a mango; the customer points at his own chest — "MY?" — voice climbing at the end the way an English question does. That climb is the question: ไหม turns any sentence into one. (↑ rising, the voice lifts like an eyebrow)
entries.headline: MY?
entries.scene: Bustling Thai street market at golden hour. A smiling vendor in an apron holds a ripe mango out across her fruit stall. Facing her, a young foreign traveller points at his own chest with both index fingers, eyebrows raised high, mouth open in an exaggerated questioning expression. Baskets of tropical fruit and hanging bulbs frame them.

entries.mnemonic: A traffic cop hands back the wallet you dropped, and the thanks is already built into the word: คุณ khun means you, so khàawp-khun is thanks-you, and the cop is standing right there to collect it. Palms together, head down, the first syllable sitting low. (▁ khàawp drops low, then khun levels out flat and mid)
entries.headline: Khàawp-khun.
entries.scene: A Bangkok street corner in the rain. A traffic policeman in a white helmet holds out a battered leather wallet to a young woman, who has stopped mid-step and pressed her palms together in front of her face, head bowed, beaming. Wet tarmac, headlights, motorbikes blurred behind them.

entries.mnemonic: A cop hands back the wallet you dropped and you press your palms together: khàawp-khun. Stretch that cop out long — khàawp — and remember what the end of it is: khun, the ordinary Thai word for you. Thanking someone is literally handing them a you. (▁ khàawp sits low, then khun levels out flat)
entries.headline: khàawp-khun.
entries.scene: A uniformed Thai police officer on a busy pavement holds out a worn leather wallet to a young woman, who has stopped mid-step and raised both hands pressed together in front of her face, head bowed, smiling. Scooters and market stalls blurred behind them in warm afternoon light.

entries.mnemonic: A crow lands on a café table, caws once, then knocks the whole tote of pastries onto the pavement. It hops down beside the mess with its wings folded and its head bowed, apologising to the entire street. CAW plus TOTE: kǎaw-thôot, the bird with better manners than most. (↓ the voice drops on the second half, the bow of the head)
entries.headline: kǎaw-thôot.
entries.scene: A glossy black crow standing on a wet pavement beside an upended canvas tote bag, pastries scattered around it, its wings folded flat and its head bowed low toward a startled woman half risen from her café chair. Overturned chair, morning light on the wet stone.

entries.mnemonic: A man backing out of a café swings his bag into a waiter and a whole rack of toast goes up in the air. On the sill a crow caws. Caw, toast. He turns round with both hands raised, wincing, saying it twice over: khǎaw-thôot. (↑ khǎaw climbs like the crow, then thôot drops as he bows)
entries.headline: Khǎaw-thôot!
entries.scene: The doorway of a small café. A man in a raincoat has just knocked a waiter's tray and slices of toast hang in the air around them both. He is turned back toward the waiter, shoulders hunched, both hands raised in apology, face screwed up. A black crow on the window ledge, beak open. Morning light.

entries.mnemonic: The same "my?" as ไหม — but shouted across a noisy bar, so the voice snaps up high and stays there instead of gliding. มั้ย is what friends say; ไหม is its polite written twin. (▲ high and flat-topped, a quick shout)
entries.headline: MY!
entries.scene: Crowded noisy Thai bar at night, packed with people. In the foreground a young man leans over a table, hands cupped around his mouth, shouting across the room toward a friend. The friend at the far side cups a hand behind his ear, squinting to hear. Coloured neon glow, condensation on beer bottles, motion and crowd blur between them.

entries.mnemonic: A man sinks into a hammock and waves lazily — "sa-baaai" — a long drowsy bye as he drifts off. Nothing hurts, nothing to do. (— the second syllable stretches out level and relaxed)
entries.headline: sa-baaai…
entries.scene: A man lying back in a woven hammock strung between two coconut palms on a quiet Thai beach, one arm hanging loose and waving a slow lazy goodbye, eyes half closed, utterly relaxed. A cold drink rests in the sand beneath him. Calm turquoise sea and soft afternoon light behind.

entries.mnemonic: ไหน and ไหม are twins with the same rising climb — only the first sound differs. ไหม (M) asks "is it so?"; ไหน (N) asks "where?". Picture two identical signposts at a fork: the M arm points at a question mark, the N arm points at a map. Same rise in the voice, different letter, different question. (↑ rising, the voice climbs as the eyes search)
entries.scene: A weathered wooden signpost at a fork in a dirt road in rural Thailand, with two identical arms pointing opposite ways. The left arm carries a large carved question mark; the right arm carries a small rolled map pinned to it. A lone traveller with a backpack stands at the fork, hand shading his eyes, looking from one arm to the other. Rice paddies and distant hills, warm late light.

entries.mnemonic: She asks for chilli and the cook reaches for the whole jar. "Nòi!" — voice dropping low as she pinches her fingers a centimetre apart. Just a bit. (▁ low and small, the voice shrinks with the gesture)
entries.headline: Nòi!
entries.scene: A street food stall. The cook, grinning, is tipping an enormous jar of dried red chilli flakes toward a bowl of noodles. Across the counter a woman lunges forward with one hand raised in alarm, her other hand pinching thumb and forefinger a tiny distance apart. Steam, woks, stacked bowls, night market lights.

entries.mnemonic: Twelve people round one table, all of them kin, every hand reaching into the same bowls at once. kin is what they are doing and who they are doing it with: you eat with your kin. One flat syllable, no fuss, used all day long. (— flat and level, an unhurried everyday word)
entries.headline: kin.
entries.scene: An extended Thai family crowded round a low table heaped with shared dishes, a dozen hands reaching in at once, a grandmother spooning rice into a small child's bowl, everyone talking over each other. A warm hanging bulb overhead, evening dark beyond the open doorway.

entries.mnemonic: A boy pulls up his shirt, pats a round full tummy and demands to know why he still has to finish the greens. Why this, why that — every one of his questions comes up out of that tummy, and none of them stops. tham-mai. (— both syllables flat and level, the drone of a child who will not give up)
entries.headline: tham-mai?
entries.scene: A small boy at a kitchen table with his shirt pulled up to his chin, both hands patting his bare round tummy, mouth open mid-question, eyebrows high. Opposite him an exhausted parent rests a chin in one hand beside a plate of untouched green vegetables. Warm evening kitchen light.

entries.mnemonic: A tow truck is hauling your car away. You sprint after it shouting "How much?! — tâo-rài!" and the driver leans out and holds up a single loaf of rye bread: that's the price. TOW plus RYE, and you never forget asking what it costs. (↓ falls hard on tâo, then drops low again on rài)
entries.headline: tâo-rài?!
entries.scene: A yellow tow truck driving away down a city street with a small car hoisted on its hook. A man in office clothes sprints after it, briefcase flying open, one arm outstretched and mouth wide open mid-shout. The driver leans out of the cab window holding up a single dark loaf of rye bread like a price tag. Motion blur, exhaust, late afternoon.

entries.mnemonic: An old janitor lifts a keyring so heavy it needs both hands — hundreds of keys fanning out like a metal peacock. Someone asks the only sensible question: "Kìi?" How many keys? (▁ low and flat, a short blunt question)
entries.headline: Kìi?
entries.scene: An elderly janitor hoists an enormous iron keyring with both hands, hundreds of keys fanned out in a glinting spray. A student beside him stares up, counting. Dim school corridor, shafts of window light.

entries.mnemonic: A cow leans over the fence into the neighbour's rye field and moos, while the farmer stands beside it with his watch open, waiting on the crop. Moo, rye. mûuea-rài asks the only thing either of them wants to know: when. Say MOO with the lips pulled wide instead of pushed forward and the Thai vowel lands. (↓ mûuea drops, then rài falls away low)
entries.headline: mûuea-rài?
entries.scene: A brown cow with its head stretched over a wooden fence into a tall golden field of rye, mouth open mid-bellow. On the near side an old farmer in a straw hat holds a pocket watch open in his palm, looking at the crop rather than the cow. Late summer haze, low sun.

entries.mnemonic: nák- is the prefix Thai sticks on the front of anyone who does a thing. Hear it as a knack — the boy with a knack for it — and glue it to riian, to study. Knack for studying: a student. Learn nák- once and it hands you a dozen other people. (— riian levels out flat and patient at the end)
entries.scene: A Thai schoolboy in a crisp white uniform sits at a wooden classroom desk, effortlessly spinning a globe on one fingertip while his classmates twist round in their seats to watch, delighted. Morning sun through louvred shutters, dust hanging in the light.

entries.mnemonic: A small boy grabs an enormous weathered hand — a bear's paw of a hand — and says "Phôo." The hand belongs to his father, and it swallows his whole fist. (↓ falling, warm and settled)
entries.headline: Phôo.
entries.scene: Close view of a small boy's hand gripping the huge weathered calloused hand of his father, whose forearm fills the frame. The boy, about five, looks up with total trust; the father, a broad Thai labourer in a faded work shirt, looks down at him with a quiet smile. Warm kitchen light, out-of-focus home interior behind.

entries.mnemonic: A cow has got her whole head into the rice cauldron and will not come out. Grains fly across the kitchen floor. The farmer's voice comes down hard — khâao! — because that is his rice, a month of it, and a cow is eating it. (↓ falling, the shout drops as it lands)
entries.headline: Khâao!
entries.scene: A rustic Thai kitchen. A cow has pushed her head deep into an enormous steaming cauldron of white rice, grains scattered across the tiled floor. A farmer in a straw hat lunges at her with both arms raised, mouth wide. Steam, morning light through a slatted window.

entries.mnemonic: A man raises his glass and intones "dɯɯm…" like a funeral bell — the last drink before DOOM. The trick is the lips: say DOOM while grinning, lips pulled wide instead of pushed forward, and you land the Thai vowel exactly. (▁ low and heavy, like the glass coming back down on the table)
entries.headline: dɯɯm…
entries.scene: A lone man at a long empty banquet table in a candlelit hall, raising a heavy glass in a solemn toast, grinning oddly wide as he does it. Behind him a huge cracked bronze bell hangs in the shadows. Guttering candles, long shadows, a sense of last things.

entries.mnemonic: He plunges both hands into the mountain stream and they go numb in seconds, that shocking cold where the fingers stop belonging to you. náam is water, and water this cold numbs. Short and high, up where the gasp is. (▲ high and taut, the sound of breath sucked in)
entries.headline: náam!
entries.scene: A young man crouched at the edge of a fast mountain stream, both hands submerged to the wrist in clear rushing water, face screwed up and mouth open in a gasp. Wet stones, spray hanging in the air, pine shadows, cold blue morning light.

entries.mnemonic: A fortune teller peers over her cards, jabs a finger at you and says "Ah — YOU!" She has guessed your age to the year. aa-yú is the number of years you have. (↓ the second syllable snaps down on YOU)
entries.headline: Ah — YOU!
entries.scene: A fortune teller's booth draped in red cloth. An old woman with rings on every finger leans across a spread of cards and jabs one finger directly at the viewer, eyes wide with certainty. On the table beside the cards sits a small ornate abacus with a row of beads pushed across. Candles, incense smoke, deep shadows.

entries.mnemonic: Two brothers stand back to back to settle who is taller. The taller one is P — top of the list — "Phîi" — and his hand comes down flat on his brother's head to prove it. (↓ falling, the hand settles the matter)
entries.headline: Phîi.
entries.scene: Two Thai brothers standing back to back in a living room, comparing heights. The taller older one has reached up and over to lay his hand flat on top of his younger brother's head, smirking. The younger one stands on tiptoe, scowling, arms folded. A doorframe behind them is marked with pencil height lines.

entries.mnemonic: The little one pipes up — "Nóng!" — high and bright, the small voice that always goes up at the end and always wants in. He is the one still waiting to grow. (▲ high, a small bright voice)
entries.headline: Nóng!
entries.scene: A small child jumping up with one arm stretched high, beaming, trying to be included in a group of older kids who are standing in a huddle above him. He is clearly the smallest by a head. Sunlit Thai schoolyard, dusty ground, green trees behind.

entries.mnemonic: Halfway across the tarmac the traveller stops, turns to the ground crew and asks which way the gate is — tǎam — the voice climbing the way every question climbs. Take the tarm off tarmac and you have the Thai for ask. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like a hand going up)
entries.headline: Tǎam?
entries.scene: An airport apron at dusk. A traveller with a wheeled case has halted mid-stride on wet tarmac and turned to a ground marshal in a hi-vis vest, palms open in a questioning gesture. The marshal points away toward distant terminal lights. Puddles, reflected glow.

entries.mnemonic: It is noon and nothing is happening. He lies flat and the afternoon goes on and on — "nooon" — never rising, never falling. (— completely level; the voice lies down too)
entries.headline: nooon…
entries.scene: A man asleep flat on his back on a wooden bench under a shop awning in the middle of a blazing hot day, hat over his face, one arm hanging off the side. A wall clock behind him reads exactly twelve. Empty sun-bleached street, hard midday shadows, heat haze.

entries.mnemonic: You suggest something ridiculous. Your friend shakes her head once and sets a heavy rock down on the table between you. Solid as a rock: no, definitely not, don't even think it. (▁ low and flat, the last word on the matter)
entries.headline: …ròok.
entries.scene: Two friends at a small café table. One leans forward mid-sentence, hands open, pleading. The other has just set a heavy grey river stone down on the tabletop between them with a thud, and is shaking her head once, eyebrows raised, utterly unmoved. Coffee cups rattle slightly. Warm café interior.

entries.mnemonic: A chef scans a row of identical mangoes, then slaps one down on the board — "nîi lɛ̀!" — that one. The word is over before it starts, cut off short like the slap itself. (▁ low and clipped, stopped dead at the end)
entries.headline: …lɛ̀!
entries.scene: A market chef's hands above a wooden board, having just slapped one mango down hard onto it; the other identical mangoes are lined up untouched behind. Slight motion blur on the striking hand, a puff of disturbed flour or dust rising from the board. Overhead market lighting, close crop.

entries.mnemonic: A woodsman too hungry to wait for the fire swings his hatchet and hews a slice straight off the ham hanging in the smokehouse, chewing while he cuts. Hew first, cook later. hǐu is the hunger that will not sit down and be patient. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like a stomach complaining)
entries.headline: hǐu!
entries.scene: A ragged woodsman in a dim smokehouse swinging a small hatchet into an enormous smoked ham hanging from a rafter, a thick slice already dropping into his other hand, both cheeks bulging. Hollow cheeks, wild eyes, an empty plate on the floor by his boot. Smoky shafts of light.

entries.mnemonic: Take STRONG and knock the S off the front: troŋ. A soldier marches dead straight down a painted line, jaw set, refusing to deviate an inch. Strong and straight are the same idea here. (— flat and level, like the line he is walking)
entries.headline: troŋ!
entries.scene: A soldier in parade uniform marching precisely along a freshly painted white line down the centre of a wide road, back rigid, gaze fixed dead ahead. The line runs away from him to a vanishing point. Onlookers stand well back on both kerbs. Bright hard sunlight, sharp shadows.

entries.mnemonic: A shopkeeper slaps a new price tag over the old one — a LOT has come off. lót is the cut itself: prices, speed, weight, volume, anything that comes down. (▲ high and sharp, the slap of the new tag going on)
entries.headline: lót!
entries.scene: A shopfront window. A grinning shopkeeper on a step stool slaps a huge red price tag over an old one, the old higher number still half visible underneath. Shoppers outside the glass are pressing in to look. Bright commercial lighting, sale banners, festive clutter.

entries.mnemonic: A rented room in a Hong Kong tower block, so small that a man standing in the middle of it reaches both walls without straightening his arms. Hong, hâawng: the room. This one is all the room there is, and the voice drops like the ceiling. (↓ falling, heavy and low)
entries.headline: hâawng.
entries.scene: A tiny high-rise flat. A man stands in the centre with both arms half raised, palms flat against opposite walls, a folded bed and a single hotplate crammed in behind him. Harsh bare bulb overhead, washing strung across one corner, city glow through a narrow slot of window.

entries.mnemonic: Ask a Thai shopkeeper what she does and she will tell you she runs this place. A ráan is a shop — the thing you run. The word and the job are the same sound. (▲ high, said with pride)
entries.headline: My ráan.
entries.scene: A proud middle-aged Thai woman standing in the open doorway of her small neighbourhood shop, arms folded, chin up, framed by shelves of goods stacked floor to ceiling behind her. A painted awning above the door, a scooter parked outside, early morning light down the street.

entries.mnemonic: Knock the P off PRAWN and you have ráawn. A fat prawn hits the grill bars and hisses, and the cook snatches his fingers back out of the flame with a yelp. Hot — the thing itself and the complaint about it, in one word. (▲ high and taut, the yelp of a burnt finger)
entries.headline: Ráawn!
entries.scene: Close on a charcoal grill at a night market: a fat prawn just dropped onto the glowing bars, flames curling up around its shell, the cook's hand jerking back with fingers splayed, his face screwed up mid-wince. Sparks, smoke, deep night behind.

entries.mnemonic: Take PRAWN and knock the P off the front: ráawn. The cook flicks prawns onto a grill so fierce they curl and hiss the instant they land, and his hand snaps back from the bars with his fingers splayed. Everything about that grill is the word. (▲ high and taut, a yelp pitched at the top of the voice)
entries.headline: ráawn!
entries.scene: A street cook at a blazing charcoal grill, prawns hitting the bars and curling instantly in a burst of flame and steam, his hand jerked back with fingers splayed wide, face screwed up. Night market, orange firelight across his skin, dark crowd behind.

entries.mnemonic: A single yen coin has been left in the freezer overnight and comes out furred with white frost, so cold it sticks to the fingertips that lift it. yen is cold, and the temperature never shifts while the voice holds it. (— flat and level, the cold does not move)
entries.headline: yen.
entries.scene: A close view of a hand holding a small coin, its face lost under white frost, fingertips pink and stuck to its surface, cold vapour spilling down from an open freezer behind. Blue-white light, ice crystals along the shelf edges, a dark kitchen beyond.

entries.mnemonic: You jàai for your chai. The two words sit almost on top of each other — the drink and the paying for it — so every cup you buy is a free rehearsal. (▁ low, the flat sound of coins going down on the counter)
entries.headline: jàai for chai.
entries.scene: A tea stall counter. A customer's hand places a small stack of coins down on the wooden counter beside a steaming glass of milky orange Thai iced tea. The vendor's hand is reaching for the coins from the other side. Close low-angle crop on the counter, warm steam, sunlit street behind.

entries.mnemonic: One spoonful and the man at the counter shuts his eyes, presses a hand flat to his chest and cannot say anything at all except à-rɔ̀y. The cook everyone on the street calls Roy points at him with the tongs. A Roy, and a review that needs no words. (▁ low, the voice drops as the eyes close)
entries.headline: à-rɔ̀y…
entries.scene: A night food stall. A diner at the counter sits with eyes squeezed shut and one hand pressed to his chest, spoon still in his mouth, an emptied bowl in front of him. The grinning cook behind the wok points at him with a pair of tongs. Steam, wok flame, strings of warm bulbs.

entries.mnemonic: Take royal and drop the -al: a-roy. A king in full robes has folded himself onto a plastic stool at a noodle cart, taken one mouthful and closed his eyes. The royal verdict on street food, and the whole court leaning in to watch him give it. (▁ the last syllable drops low and satisfied)
entries.headline: à-ròi!
entries.scene: A king in an embroidered robe and gold circlet perched on a low plastic stool at a night-market noodle cart, eyes closed in bliss, a laden spoon halfway to his mouth. The vendor grins over her steaming pot; two courtiers in uniform wait awkwardly behind. Hanging bulbs, steam, dark street.

entries.mnemonic: The crowd goes rah as the car turns slowly on its stand, and a buyer at the rail holds up a fat brick of banknotes. raa-khaa — a rah and a car — is what the thing costs, and it is the one thing everybody came to hear. (— both syllables flat and level, a price stated plainly)
entries.headline: raa-khaa?
entries.scene: A motor show hall. A gleaming saloon revolves slowly on a turntable under white spotlights while a ring of onlookers cheer with arms raised. At the rail a buyer in a linen suit holds a thick brick of banknotes above his head.

entries.mnemonic: Every career ladder has the same thing at the top: a chief. aa-chîip is the whole ladder — the trade you follow and where it leads. (↓ falls firmly on the second syllable, the weight of a title)
entries.headline: aa-chîip.
entries.scene: A long ladder rising out of an open-plan office floor and up through a skylight, with workers in different uniforms — cook, nurse, mechanic, engineer — climbing it at different heights. At the very top rung stands a figure in a chief's peaked cap, silhouetted against bright sky. Upward perspective.

entries.mnemonic: At the wedding feast the couple's wrists are bound together with white cord and they feed each other from one torn round of naan. Say TANG NAAN and let the ng of tang run straight on into naan — one bread, one sound, two people joined. (— the second syllable holds level and long, like the vow)
entries.headline: dtàaeng-ngaan.
entries.scene: A wedding feast under strung lights. A bride and groom sit close with their wrists bound together by a loop of white cord, each lifting a torn piece of flatbread to the other's mouth, both laughing. Guests lean in around a crowded table. Warm evening light, petals on the cloth.

entries.mnemonic: The waiter refuses to take a spoken order — everything must be sung. The customer stands, hand on heart, and sings her dinner across the restaurant. You sàng what you sung. (▁ low and flat, even when sung badly)
entries.headline: sàng!
entries.scene: A restaurant dining room. A woman has risen from her table, one hand on her heart and the other flung out theatrically, singing her order toward a waiter who stands to attention with notepad raised, delighted. Other diners turn to watch. Warm chandelier light, white tablecloths.

entries.mnemonic: ใกล้ klâi and ไกล klai are the same handful of sounds and only the tone separates them. The falling one is the one that comes down to you: a bird dropping onto an outstretched hand. The level one keeps going, out to the horizon. Near falls. Far stays flat. (↓ falling, the bird lands on the hand)
entries.headline: klâi.
entries.scene: A woman standing in an open field with one arm held out, a small bird just settling onto her fingers, wings still spread. Far behind her a second bird is a tiny speck against a pale sky above distant hills. Early morning, long grass, soft light.

entries.mnemonic: Say poo-an, but grinning — lips pulled wide instead of pushed forward — and you land the Thai vowel exactly: phûuean. Two friends with their arms round each other's shoulders, both grinning like that, are the word and the way to say it in one picture. (↓ falling, warm, the voice settles)
entries.headline: phûuean.
entries.scene: Two young men on a beach at sunset with their arms slung round each other's shoulders, heads tipped together, both grinning enormously with lips pulled wide, sand on their knees, a football at their feet. Low orange sun flaring behind them, long shadows.

entries.mnemonic: Whatever you bought, you bought it in bàat. The English past tense and the Thai currency are the same sound, and the one always follows the other. (▁ low and flat, the sound of a note being laid down)
entries.headline: bàat.
entries.scene: A close overhead view of a market transaction: a hand laying purple and green Thai banknotes down onto a wooden counter, beside a wrapped parcel tied with string that has just been paid for. The vendor's hands rest on the parcel, about to push it across. Warm stall lighting.

entries.mnemonic: The spoon comes toward the child and he opens his mouth — not to swallow, but to let out one long flat yaaa that goes on until his breath runs out. The syrup goes in anyway. Every dose starts with that noise, and that noise is the word. (— flat and level, held as long as his lungs allow)
entries.headline: yaaa…
entries.scene: A small child on a sofa with his head tipped back and his mouth wide open in a full-throated howl, both fists clenched. A parent leans in with a spoonful of dark red syrup in one hand and a small brown bottle in the other. Scattered toys, lamp-lit living room.

entries.mnemonic: Say the first syllable of plaza and stop there: plah. A silver fish the length of a man has come up out of the fountain in the town plaza and is flapping about on the flagstones while the whole square backs away from it. plaa is the fish. (— flat and level, said plainly)
entries.headline: plaa!
entries.scene: A paved town square at midday with an ornate fountain at its centre. An enormous silver fish lies flapping on the wet flagstones beside it, water spreading around it, spray still falling. A ring of startled people has backed away, one child pointing. Hard sunlight, pigeons scattering.

entries.mnemonic: A fat carp works its mouth against the glass — blah, blah, blah — silent, endless, never changing pitch. bplaa is fish, and the fish stands there saying its own name at you all afternoon. (— flat and level, one long unchanging blah)
entries.headline: blah, blah.
entries.scene: Close on a fat orange carp pressed against aquarium glass, mouth wide open mid-gulp, one round eye staring out. On the other side of the glass a bored child rests her chin on the rim, watching it. Green-lit water, rising bubbles.

entries.mnemonic: A glider slips its tow rope and simply keeps going — over the ridge, over the river, until it is a speck a watcher has to squint at. Say GLIDE and drop the d: glai. Whatever it is, it is a long way off. (— flat and level, the word carries without any effort at all)
entries.headline: glai.
entries.scene: A white sailplane far out over a vast green valley, tiny against an enormous sky, its tow rope falling away beneath it. On a grassy ridge in the foreground a figure shades their eyes with one hand, watching it shrink toward distant blue mountains. Late afternoon light, huge depth.

entries.mnemonic: The bride has lost hers somewhere in a reception of two hundred guests, so she calls across the room. One man stands up in the middle of the tables, hand high, thumb jabbing at his own chest: saa, ME. A long open aah, then ME. That is the husband. (↑ sǎa climbs as the hand goes up, then mii sits flat)
entries.headline: saa— ME.
entries.scene: A crowded wedding reception. A bride in white stands on a chair scanning the room, and among the seated guests one man in a dinner jacket has risen, one hand high, the other thumb pointed at his own chest, grinning. Everyone else is turned toward him. Chandeliers, round tables, warm light.

entries.mnemonic: Take a nun, add a g, and sit her down: nâng. In Thai you do not ride a bus, you sit it — nâng rót — so the word for sitting is also the word for riding. She drops onto the bench and the truck pulls away. (↓ falling, the weight of someone landing on a wooden bench)
entries.headline: nâng.
entries.scene: The open back of a red songthaew truck bumping along a country road, a nun in a white habit seated on the wooden bench among baskets of vegetables, one hand gripping the rail, her veil lifting in the wind. Dusty green roadside, low sun.

entries.mnemonic: Soon, says the engineer, and the count runs down to nothing. sǔun is zero, and his fingers make the empty circle at the very moment the rocket goes. Soon arrives, the count empties out, and that emptiness is the word. (↑ rising, the voice climbs as the count runs out)
entries.headline: Sǔun.
entries.scene: A dim mission control room at night. An engineer leans back from a glowing console, one hand raised making a circle with thumb and forefinger, eyes on the wide window where a rocket lifts off its pad in a bloom of white exhaust.

entries.mnemonic: A cat on a windowsill lifts its nose, reads the air and knows the rain is coming an hour before you do. aa-kàat is both the air and what it is doing — weather. (▁ the second syllable settles low, like the cat)
entries.headline: aa-kàat.
entries.scene: A cat sitting upright on an open wooden windowsill, nose lifted and eyes half closed, whiskers catching the wind. Beyond the window a dark bank of monsoon cloud is rolling in over rooftops while the street below is still in sunshine. Curtains lifting in the draught.

entries.mnemonic: A cat strolls along the table edge and calmly nudges a tumbler into the void. CAT — OW! — and the glass is gone. Say those two together and you have kɛ̂ɛo. (↓ falls, the way the glass does)
entries.headline: CAT — OW!
entries.scene: A cat on a dining table extends one paw, pushing a drinking glass off the edge; the glass tumbles in mid-air below, water arcing out. Sunlit wooden dining room, shallow focus.

entries.mnemonic: Sunrise, and he crouches in the doorway on ONE KNEE to lace his boots before the light is properly up. Not next week, not tomorrow — this day, the one starting now, wan-níi. One knee on the threshold of it. (▲ the second half snaps up high and taut, sharp as the first light)
entries.headline: wan-níi.
entries.scene: A man crouched on one knee in an open doorway, tying the laces of a work boot, head lifted toward a low orange sun rising over rooftops. Long shadows stretch back into the dim hallway behind him. Cool blue interior, warm gold spilling across the threshold.

entries.mnemonic: She lifts a tiny gold ring off the velvet and the jeweller calmly builds the stack of banknotes it will cost beside it, a stack taller than the ring is wide. The pang goes straight through her chest. phaaeng: expensive. (— flat and level, the price is not negotiable)
entries.headline: phaaeng.
entries.scene: A jeweller's counter under bright spotlights. A small gold ring sits on a velvet pad; beside it the jeweller has built a tall stack of banknotes. The customer has one hand pressed flat to her chest, leaning back, eyes wide. Glass cases, reflections, hushed shop interior.

entries.mnemonic: Dawn in a camp: the cook bangs a ladle on the pot and the whole sleepy line shuffles up for chow. Breakfast is the first thing that happens in a Thai morning, and cháaw is the morning itself. (▲ high and bright, a shout across a cold yard)
entries.headline: Cháaw!
entries.scene: Dawn in a field camp. A cook in an apron ladles steaming rice porridge into the tin bowls of a queue of sleepy workers, their breath showing in the cold. Pink light over a misty field, smoke rising from a fire behind them.

entries.mnemonic: The doctor holds the stethoscope to a man's back and keeps circling one finger: more breath, and more, and more. Say MORE the British way, with no r on the end, and you have mǎaw — the one person who always wants another deep breath out of you. (↑ rising, climbing like the eyebrows above the mask)
entries.headline: mǎaw.
entries.scene: A doctor in a white coat pressing a stethoscope to the bare back of a seated patient, one finger raised and circling to ask for another breath. The patient's chest is swelled with held air, eyes wide. Bright clinic room, paper-covered couch, cool daylight from a high window.

entries.mnemonic: The doctor tips a spoonful of syrup into the boy and, before he has finished swallowing, is already filling the spoon again. More. More rest, more water, more of this. mǎaw is the doctor, and more is what she always wants. (↑ rising, the voice lifts with the spoon)
entries.headline: mǎaw: more.
entries.scene: A small clinic room. A doctor in a white coat with a stethoscope round her neck holds a brimming spoon of dark syrup toward a boy on the examination couch, the bottle in her other hand already tilted to refill it. The boy is pulling back, cheeks bulging. Bright clean daylight.

entries.mnemonic: Nah — the tea is not ready, it wants another minute. naa-thii is that gap exactly: the sand running through while the leaves open and nobody does anything useful. Nah, tea. Sixty seconds and not a second less. (— both syllables flat, the way a minute just sits there)
entries.headline: naa-thii.
entries.scene: A kitchen counter in morning light. A squat teapot steams beside a small hourglass timer, its sand halfway run through. A woman leans on folded arms at the counter, chin resting on her wrists, watching the sand fall, an empty mug beside her.

entries.mnemonic: The driving instructor has given up. Every time the learner drifts the wrong way he tips his head back, lets out a long theatrical sigh and jabs his thumb over his own left shoulder. Sigh, and point left: sáai. (▲ high and taut, the pitch of a man at the end of his patience)
entries.headline: sáai!
entries.scene: The inside of a small car seen from the back seat. The instructor in the passenger seat slumps with his head tipped back and eyes shut, cheeks puffed in a long exhale, thumb jabbed back over his own left shoulder. The learner grips the wheel, glancing sideways. Flat grey daylight through the windscreen.

entries.mnemonic: The lifeboat is going down by the stern, so over the side go the suitcases, the chairs, the oars, everything. What he will not let go of is one dented tin can of water held hard against his chest. Some can. sǎm-khan is the thing that actually matters. (↑ sǎm climbs, then khan lands flat and certain)
entries.headline: sǎm-khan.
entries.scene: An overloaded wooden lifeboat low in a grey swell. A man at the stern heaves a suitcase over the side with one arm while the other clamps a dented tin can tight against his chest. Other passengers cling to the gunwales, soaked. Heavy cloud, spray, cold light.

entries.mnemonic: An electrician holds his meter up to a bare bulb to see how many watts it is pulling, and the needle swings across and settles. wát is that act — measuring, finding out how much of a thing there actually is. (▲ high and tight, the needle flicking up the dial)
entries.headline: wát.
entries.scene: A dim workshop. An electrician on a wooden stepladder holds a handheld meter up toward a bare bulb hanging on a cable, its needle mid-swing across a round dial, his face lit warm from below by the filament. Shadowed rafters and coiled cable behind.

entries.mnemonic: A traveller points up at a gold-spired roof over a courtyard wall and turns up his palm: what is that? The old guide beside him only nods once and says wát. Question and answer are the same sound, and the answer is always a temple. (▲ high and taut, cut off short by the last consonant)
entries.headline: Wát.
entries.scene: A gold-spired Thai temple roof rising behind a courtyard wall. In front, a traveller with a camera points up at it with one arm, mouth open, the other palm turned up in a shrug, while an elderly guide beside him simply nods, hands clasped. Hot white sky, a monk in saffron passing behind.

entries.mnemonic: The lek hiding in the middle of electron is the Thai word for small — and an electron is the smallest thing anyone has ever bothered to name. A man stands in a hall of vast machinery built entirely to look at one speck. (▲ high and taut, said fast, a tiny word)
entries.headline: lék.
entries.scene: A cavernous laboratory hall filled with enormous copper coils and pipework. A physicist in a white coat stands dwarfed at the centre, bending to peer at a single minuscule point of blue light suspended between two great metal plates. Cold industrial lighting, deep shadows.

entries.mnemonic: The chow bell goes at the end of harvest and the whole village comes: grandmothers, farmhands, babies on hips, every last one of them holding a bowl. ชาว is not a crowd, it is the folk of a place, the people of somewhere, and chow brings all of them out at once. (— flat and level, one long even call)
entries.headline: chaao!
entries.scene: A village clearing at dusk with a long trestle of steaming pots. A hundred villagers of every age converge on it from the fields and houses, bowls in hand, some running, an old woman carried between two grandsons. Lanterns strung overhead, dust in the air, last orange light.

entries.mnemonic: Mark my— and he never finishes the sentence, because the crowd coming through the gate is past counting. mâak-maai is more than anyone can mark: many, plenty, loads of the stuff. (↓ falls hard on mâak, then maai levels out flat)
entries.headline: Mâak-maai!
entries.scene: A man stands on a wooden crate at the edge of a temple fairground, arm half raised and mouth open mid-sentence, overwhelmed as an enormous crowd streams past him in every direction and fills the frame to the horizon. Evening lanterns, dust in the air.

entries.mnemonic: Say RUCKSACK and drop the last k: rák-sǎa. His is twenty years old, a quilt of mismatched patches, every strap restitched a dozen times, and he is sewing another patch on now rather than buying a new one. That keeping-a-thing-going is the word. (↑ the second half climbs, the lift of the pack going back on)
entries.headline: rák-sǎa.
entries.scene: An old hiker sitting on a boulder, sewing a fresh patch onto a battered canvas rucksack balanced across his knees, needle raised mid-stitch, small round glasses low on his nose. The pack is a quilt of mismatched patches and re-stitched straps. A mountain trail behind, cold clear morning light.

entries.mnemonic: The fairground strongman brings the mallet down and the puck goes all the way up the tower: the bell at the top rang, and rang loud enough to stop the music. แรง is that. Force, power, the strength that made the bell speak. (— flat and level, held like a struck note)
entries.headline: …and it RANG.
entries.scene: A night fairground high striker. A heavily built man in a vest has just swung a mallet onto the pad, the puck streaking up the tower, and the brass bell at the top is jolting sideways mid-strike. A small crowd flinches back, lit by strings of coloured bulbs.

entries.mnemonic: The whole village turns out for the harvest supper: every family at one long table down the middle of the barn, bowls going hand to hand over the heads of the children. Chow, in a barn. That crowd — not the town, not the government, the people of the place — is chaao-bâan. (↓ falling, the weight of the word comes down on bâan)
entries.headline: chaao-bâan.
entries.scene: The inside of a large timber barn at dusk, one long trestle table running its length with forty villagers of every age crowded along both sides, bowls of food passing hand to hand. Children underneath the table, a dog, hay bales to the rafters. Lantern light, blue evening through the open doors.

entries.mnemonic: Say the first syllable of kayak and stop there: kǎai. A river trader has eight of them roped nose to tail along the bank and is holding a ninth over his head, shouting across the water at the tourists. Whatever he has, he sells it. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the arms)
entries.headline: kǎai!
entries.scene: A muddy riverbank lined with brightly painted kayaks roped nose to tail. A wiry trader in shorts stands on an upturned hull holding one small kayak above his head with both arms, shouting across the water toward a group of tourists on the far bank. Hot bright midday, brown river.

entries.mnemonic: Climbing out of the taxi you count coins into the driver's palm: the kʰâa, what the ride costs. It is the same khaa that ends raa-khaa, price — said on its own now, with the voice dropping as each coin goes down. (↓ falling, the drop of money leaving your hand)
entries.headline: khâa.
entries.scene: A night street, a taxi stopped at the kerb with its rear door open. A passenger leans to the driver's window counting coins one by one into his open palm, dashboard glow on both their faces, wet tarmac reflecting neon behind them.

entries.mnemonic: A great ape with heavy jowls sits on the summit of a heap of crates and bicycles, one fist thumping his chest and one arm spread over the lot of it. Every last item is his. Run JOWL into KONG and you have jâo-kǎwng: the one it all belongs to. (↑ the second half climbs, the pitch of a claim being staked)
entries.headline: jâo-kǎwng!
entries.scene: An enormous gorilla with heavy jowls seated on top of a mountain of crates, bicycles and furniture inside a warehouse, one fist mid-thump against his chest, the other arm flung wide over the heap. Small figures on the floor far below crane up at him. Dusty shafts of light from high windows.

entries.mnemonic: Mum points, arm dead straight, at the place where the two walls meet, and the boy goes and stands in it. That exact meeting of two walls is the mum: the corner, the angle. Nobody argues with the arm. (— flat and level, no rise, no give)
entries.headline: mum.
entries.scene: A plain sitting room. A woman stands with her arm extended rigidly toward the corner where two walls meet; a small boy trudges toward it with his head down and one sock falling. Afternoon light through net curtains, an armchair pushed aside.

entries.mnemonic: The stylist keeps adding rollers to the perm — one more, one more, pʰɤ̂ɤm — until the head is twice the size it started. pʰɤ̂ɤm is to add on top of what is already there: more curls, more chilli, more money. (↓ falling and firm, another roller clamped on)
entries.headline: pʰɤ̂ɤm!
entries.scene: A salon chair under warm bulb-framed mirrors. A woman's head is piled absurdly high with dozens of coloured curlers, and the stylist leans in with yet another one held ready in her fingers, both of them laughing at the size of it.

entries.mnemonic: He ducks under the table after a dropped coin and comes up short — his tie is pinned beneath the table leg and his neck will go no further. Under the table is where the tie is, and where he now lives. tâi. (↓ falling, the word drops with him)
entries.headline: tâi.
entries.scene: A man in a suit on hands and knees half beneath a heavy dining table, his neck yanked sideways because his necktie is trapped under one of the table legs. A dropped coin glints just past his fingertips. Guests' shoes and hems all around him. Low floor-level view, warm dining light above.

entries.mnemonic: Two doves on a wire, turned toward each other, cooing — khûu, khûu — and the rest of the wire completely empty. A khûu is a pair: never one, always two, and they only make that sound together. (↓ falling, the drop at the end of a dove's call)
entries.headline: khûu…
entries.scene: Two white doves perched side by side on a telephone wire against a pale dawn sky, heads turned toward one another, throats puffed out mid-call. The wire runs away empty in both directions. Soft cold light, a rooftop far below.

entries.mnemonic: A monk steps off the kerb into six lanes of traffic and walks straight across without once hurrying, robes barely stirring, and the whole road stops for him. Calm is how he crosses, and CALM the British way, with the l silent, is how the word sounds. (↓ falling, steady and unhurried)
entries.headline: kâam.
entries.scene: A saffron-robed monk walking unhurried across a wide city road, hands folded, robes stirring in the wash of halted traffic. Cars, taxis and motorbikes stopped in both directions, drivers leaning out to watch him. Heat shimmer, exhaust haze, hard tropical sun.

entries.mnemonic: Sue stands in the middle of the room and the room comes to her: the rug rucking up, the chairs walking on their legs, an orange rolling across the boards. Everything goes to Sue. sùu is that word and nothing more. To, towards, into. (▁ low and flat, a short word that only points)
entries.headline: …sùu Sue.
entries.scene: A living room where the furniture is sliding across the floorboards toward a woman standing calmly in the centre, arms at her sides. A rug rucks up at her feet, two chairs tilt toward her mid-slide, an orange rolls across the boards. Lamplight, slightly tilted framing.

entries.mnemonic: Prom night: the doors swing open and the whole class steps out in one movement, dressed and ready. pʰrɔ́ɔm is both halves of that — ready, and all at the same moment. (▲ high and taut, the held beat before everyone moves)
entries.headline: Pʰrɔ́ɔm!
entries.scene: The double doors of a school hall flung open at night, warm light spilling out behind a line of teenagers in formal dress stepping down onto the steps in perfect unison, mid-stride, chins up. Dark sky, camera flashes popping from the crowd below.

entries.mnemonic: This one is built, not borrowed. rúu on its own is to know. Stretch it into rúu-sùek and the knowing leaves the head and drops into the body: a woman stops in a doorway with her hand flat on her chest, knowing a thing before she has any words for it. Knowing, felt. (▁ the second syllable falls low and short, a knock under the ribs)
entries.headline: rúu-sùek.
entries.scene: A woman standing motionless in a kitchen doorway with one hand pressed flat over her heart and her eyes lowered, caught in the instant of registering something. A phone lies face down on the counter behind her. Late afternoon light through the window, the rest of the room quiet and still.

entries.mnemonic: The doctor asks which one is hurting and he smacks his own knee twice, hard: nîi. This one. Not that one, not the one from last year, this knee, the one he can reach and hit. นี่ always points at whatever is nearest to hand. (↓ falling, the voice drops with the hand)
entries.headline: Nîi.
entries.scene: A clinic examination room. A man sitting on the couch with both trouser legs rolled up slaps his own left knee with a flat palm, caught mid-strike, jaw set. The doctor leans in with a small torch, eyebrows up. Bright clinical light, paper-covered couch.

entries.mnemonic: She asked for one carrot. The grocer hands over a pack so enormous she has to hug it with both arms, greens bursting out of the top and over her face, the single carrot still held up in her fingers. A whole pack of phàk. (▁ low and clipped, stopped dead by the k)
entries.headline: phàk!
entries.scene: A small woman in a market staggering backwards under an enormous wrapped pack of vegetables held in both arms, leafy greens bursting out of the top and across her face, one carrot pinched between her fingers. The grocer behind the stall grins with his hands on his hips. Bright morning market, stacked crates.

entries.mnemonic: On the museum shelf the heart comes first and the lung in the jar comes after it, always after, never before. Lung, jar: lǎng-jàak. Hear the lid click shut on the end of jàak, and remember that หลัง on its own means behind. (↑ lǎng climbs, then jàak drops low and clipped)
entries.headline: lǎng-jàak.
entries.scene: A dim museum shelf of specimen jars. A curator's gloved hand rests on the second jar, which holds a pale lung suspended in fluid; the first jar beside it holds a heart. A brass lamp throws a warm pool of light and the rest of the cabinet falls into shadow.

entries.mnemonic: Yin is the female half of the old pair. Finish it the way English finishes sing and you have jǐŋ, the word for female. A dancer turns slowly out of the light and into the dark, half bright and half shadow, all in one movement. (↑ rising, the voice climbs with the turn)
entries.headline: jǐŋ.
entries.scene: A dark stage. A Thai dancer in a gold headdress and long silk skirt turns slowly mid-movement, her curved fingers and the sweep of her skirt tracing a circle; one half of her lit warm, the other lost in shadow.

entries.mnemonic: The head teacher refuses to announce it to the room. She goes along the row and tells one child, then the next, then the next — tell a, tell a, tell a — until every single one of them has had it from her own mouth. tɛ̀ɛ-lá: each, taken one at a time. (▲ the second syllable snaps up high and stops dead)
entries.headline: tɛ̀ɛ-lá.
entries.scene: A school hall with a long row of seated children. A head teacher crouches beside one of them with a hand cupped to the child's ear, mid-whisper, while the children further down the row lean forward waiting their turn. Tall windows, dust hanging in the light, polished floorboards.

entries.mnemonic: He has turned the kitchen out looking for his tea: cupboard doors hanging open, tins on the floor, still no cup. Tea, where? ที่ marks the place and ไหน asks which one, so thîi-nǎi is simply which place. (↓ thîi drops, then nǎi climbs as his eyes come up)
entries.headline: Tea — thîi-nǎi?
entries.scene: A small kitchen turned upside down: every cupboard door hanging open, tins and jars crowding the worktop and the floor. A man stands in the middle of it with both palms turned up and his shoulders raised, staring at an empty shelf. Morning light, a cold kettle on the hob.

entries.mnemonic: The sweep climbs down off the last chimney on the terrace, black with soot, and pulls his crooked tie straight. Soot and tie: sùt-tʰáai, the final one, the end of the row with nothing after it. (▲ tʰáai lifts high, the voice rising on the last of them)
entries.headline: sùt-tʰáai.
entries.scene: Dusk on a long terrace rooftop. A soot-blackened chimney sweep stands on the very last chimney pot of a row that recedes into the distance, straightening his crooked tie, brushes slung over one shoulder. Orange sun low behind the rooftops, smoke drifting.

entries.mnemonic: Squeeze PLAYING down into one syllable — playng — and you have pleeng. A busker on the same corner with the same battered guitar has been playing the same thing for years, and by now the man and the song have grown into each other. (— level and even, held like a sustained note)
entries.headline: pleeng.
entries.scene: A street busker on a corner with a battered acoustic guitar, head tipped back and eyes shut mid-song, one foot tapping beside an open instrument case. A loose half-circle of passers-by has stopped, one child swaying. Evening city light, wet pavement throwing back shopfront glow.

entries.mnemonic: The great ape is still up on the tower, decades on, still young, still refusing to come down. Young Kong: jaŋ-kʰoŋ is still — not motionless, but unstopped, carrying on exactly as it was. (— both syllables flat and level, nothing has changed)
entries.headline: jaŋ-kʰoŋ.
entries.scene: A giant gorilla clinging to the spire of a skyscraper at dawn, one arm hooked round the mast, chest heaving, mist and rooftops far below. Pigeons wheel round him and one sits on his shoulder, entirely at home. Cold pink light.

entries.mnemonic: Put an R in front of ORB: rɔ̂ɔp. In the lighthouse the great glass orb turns all night on its bearing, flinging the same beam over the same black water, round after round after round, and it will still be doing it at dawn. (↓ falling, the beam drops away as it swings past)
entries.headline: rɔ̂ɔp.
entries.scene: The lamp room of a lighthouse at night: an enormous glowing glass lens assembly turning on its bearing, one broad beam flung out across black sea and rocks far below. A keeper stands small beside it with a hand on the rail, his face lit and then dark. Deep night blue, hot amber light.

entries.thai: ความรู้สึก
entries.mnemonic: A qualm is a feeling that will not sit still, and kʰwaam is how the Thai starts. kʰwaam- is the noun-maker: stick it on rúu-sɯ̀k, to sense, and you get the sensing itself — the feeling. Qualm first, every time. (▁ the last syllable sinks low, the way a qualm settles in the stomach)
entries.headline: kʰwaam-rúu-sɯ̀k.
entries.scene: A man alone at a kitchen table late at night, one hand pressed flat against his stomach, brow furrowed, staring past an untouched bowl of rice. A single bulb on a cord swings very slightly above him, shadows tilting across the wall.

entries.mnemonic: A ship's hawser, thick as a man's arm, has frayed at the tip, and every ply of it springs loose in the sailor's hands like the bristles of a brush. The plaai is the far end — the point where a thing runs out and stops. (— flat and level, the rope running out)
entries.headline: plaai.
entries.scene: A close view of a sailor's weathered hands holding the frayed tip of a thick ship's rope, its separate strands sprung loose in every direction like a brush. Behind him the rope runs away taut across a wet deck toward a bollard. Grey sea light, salt spray in the air.

entries.mnemonic: A cat stretched the full length of a garden wall lets out a yowl that will not end, one flat note going on and on over the rooftops. Drop the L and there it is: yaao, long. The cat is long and the note is longer. (— dead level; the pitch never moves, it just keeps going)
entries.headline: yaaaao…
entries.scene: A long ginger cat stretched out at full length along the top of a garden wall at night, head back, mouth open in a howl. Rooftops and chimney pots recede behind it under a low moon; a light has come on in a window across the yard.

entries.mnemonic: Knock the O off TANGO and you have tɛ̀ng. Nobody dances a tango in their work clothes: the word is getting dressed, arranged, put together properly. The same verb composes a song — cloth or music, it is all arranging. (▁ low and flat, the pause before the music starts)
entries.headline: tɛ̀ng.
entries.scene: A dressing room doorway. A woman in a fitted scarlet dance dress stands with arms raised while an older dresser kneels to pin her hem; beside her a man in a black suit adjusts his cuffs. Beyond them a lit dance floor waits.

entries.mnemonic: The child on the trolley is terrified, so the anaesthetist leans down and sings to her — quietly, badly — right up to the moment she goes under. She sang, then the op, and between the two of them everything went completely still. Say SANG OP and let the ng slide across. (▁ low and flat, the voice settling to nothing)
entries.headline: sà-ngòp.
entries.scene: A hospital corridor. An anaesthetist in scrubs bends over a child lying on a trolley, one hand holding hers, mouth open in quiet song. The child's eyes are half closed and her other hand has gone limp. Behind them the theatre doors stand open, spilling hard white light into the dim corridor.

entries.mnemonic: A small son stands at the chai stall with his mouth open, following the long ribbon of tea as the vendor pours it from a pot held high into one held low. He has forgotten his own cup entirely. Son, chai: sǒn-jai is exactly that, your attention gone somewhere else. (↑ sǒn climbs, then jai lands flat where his eyes are)
entries.headline: sǒn-jai.
entries.scene: A street chai stall at dusk. A vendor pours a long ribbon of milky tea from a pot held high into another held low, steam curling off it. A boy of about seven stands at the counter, chin tilted up, mouth open, utterly transfixed, his own cup untouched beside him.

entries.mnemonic: Every morning at the same hour he packs a tea into the same dented flask and takes the same seat on the same bus. pà-kà-tì — pack a tea — is the way things normally are: ordinary, usual, nothing out of place. (▁ low and flat throughout, nothing remarkable happens)
entries.headline: pà-kà-tì.
entries.scene: A small kitchen at dawn. A middle-aged man in a work shirt spoons tea into a dented steel flask; his lunch tin, coat and keys are laid out on the table in exactly their usual places. Grey early light, everything worn and familiar.

entries.mnemonic: Put a D on the front of EARN, said the British way with no r in it: dəən. He walks the four miles to the yard every morning because the bus fare would come out of what he earns. Every step is walked and every step is earned. (— flat and level, the rhythm of a long walk)
entries.headline: dəən.
entries.scene: A man in work clothes walking a long empty country road at dawn, a lunch tin swinging from one hand, his breath showing in the cold. The road runs on to a distant industrial yard on the horizon. Frost on the verges, low pink sun behind him, his shadow stretched far ahead.

entries.mnemonic: The gallery is silent. The artist's arm juts out, the brush touches the huge white canvas once, and that is the whole painting: one black dot in the middle of all that space. jùt is the dot. A jab, and stop. (▁ low and clipped, over as soon as it starts)
entries.headline: jùt.
entries.scene: A white gallery wall holding one enormous blank canvas with a single small black dot at its centre. The artist stands close, arm still thrust forward, a fine brush in hand, the paint still wet. Two visitors watch from the far side of the polished floor. Cool even gallery light.

entries.mnemonic: She walks the line of her class the way a captain walks the deck in front of a crew — khruu, crew, the one who keeps the whole lot upright and moving in the same direction. One flat syllable, said with respect. (— flat and level, unhurried)
entries.headline: Khruu.
entries.scene: A sunlit Thai schoolyard. A teacher in a neat uniform walks slowly along a line of pupils standing to attention, hands clasped behind her back, inspecting them; the children stand straight-backed, one sneaking a grin. Dusty ground, green trees, hard morning light.

entries.mnemonic: Put an S in front of OAT and stop there: sòot. One man, one bowl of oats, one spoon, at a table laid for one, with five chairs still tucked in. Nobody to cook for and nobody cooking for him. (▁ low and flat, as small as the bowl)
entries.headline: sòot.
entries.scene: A man sitting alone at one end of a long kitchen table eating porridge from a single bowl, one chair pulled out and five others tucked in. A single mug and spoon on the drainer behind him. Grey morning light through a bare window, the room quiet and still.

entries.thai: ยินดีที่ได้รู้จัก
entries.mnemonic: ยินดี yin-dii is gladness: the two halves of the yin symbol clicking together, and ดี dii genuinely does mean good. The tail of the phrase, rúu-jàk, is knowing someone. Glad to have come to know you, and the whole thing lasts exactly one handshake. (— yin-dii sits flat and warm, then the end drops low on jàk)
entries.headline: yin-dii…
entries.scene: Two men meeting in a hotel lobby, hands clasped in a firm handshake, both leaning in slightly, genuinely pleased. Beneath their feet the polished floor carries a large circular inlay of two interlocking black and white teardrops. Tall windows, soft morning light, a plant in a brass pot.

entries.thai: คุณสบายดีไหม
entries.mnemonic: Four pieces you already own: khun, you; sà-baai, comfortable; dii, good; and mǎi, the little hook that turns anything into a question. Stack them in that order and you have asked after somebody's health. Nothing new to learn here, only the order. (↑ rising, the voice lifts on mǎi right at the end)
entries.headline: …sà-baai dii mǎi?
entries.scene: Two neighbours meeting on a narrow village lane in the morning. One clasps the other's hand in both of hers and leans in, eyebrows raised, mouth open mid-question, smiling warmly; the other smiles back. Laundry strung overhead, sunlight through leaves.

entries.mnemonic: Three pieces you already own, laid end to end. chǎn is I. sà-baai is the man in the hammock waving his long lazy bye. dii is good. Say them in that order and you have answered the question honestly: I am comfortable, and that is good. (— the last word lands flat and level, no fuss in it)
entries.headline: chǎn sà-baai dii.
entries.scene: A woman in the doorway of a small house, one hand raised in an easy wave to a neighbour across the lane, shoulders loose, an unhurried smile. A hammock hangs on the veranda behind her. Late afternoon sun, washing on a line, everything settled.

entries.mnemonic: Ben swings round with a glass of rye and puts the whole thing down your front. You look at the stain, look at Ben, and wave it away: mâi-bpen-rai. My, Ben, rye. Never mind, it is nothing, it is okay. (↓ mâi drops hard, then the last two float off flat)
entries.headline: mâi-bpen-rai.
entries.scene: A crowded wooden bar. A man has just turned with a tumbler and sloshed dark spirit down the front of another man's shirt; the glass is still tipped in his hand, his face frozen in horror. The soaked man is laughing, one hand raised palm out, entirely unbothered. Warm amber light, bottles behind.

entries.mnemonic: A man at the bar holds one finger up over the crowd. Say noong — but grinning, lips pulled wide rather than rounded — and you land the Thai vowel: nɯ̀ng. One finger, one beer, one short low syllable. (▁ low and short, over almost before it starts)
entries.headline: Nɯ̀ng!
entries.scene: A crowded bar counter at night. A man leans in with one index finger raised high above the heads around him, grinning broadly with his lips pulled wide; the barman is already reaching for a glass. Bottles glinting on shelves, warm low light.

entries.mnemonic: Two singers, one song. Neither will start without the other and neither can carry it alone, so they stand at the same microphone with their heads turned toward each other and take the same breath. sǎwng is two, and it sounds exactly like the thing it takes both of them to make. (↑ rising, the pitch climbs as they draw breath)
entries.headline: sǎwng.
entries.scene: Two singers side by side at a single microphone on a small stage, heads turned toward each other, mouths open on the same note, one hand each resting on the stand. A warm spotlight, a dark hall, two long shadows thrown back across the boards.

entries.mnemonic: The choir stalls seat sixty and three choristers have turned up. They sing the psalm anyway, and the one on the end holds up three fingers to count them all in. Psalm, sǎam, three: the hymn and the number come out of the mouth the same way. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the three fingers)
entries.headline: sǎam.
entries.scene: A vast stone church interior with rows of empty carved choir stalls. Three choristers in red robes stand together in the middle of one row, mouths open in song; the nearest holds up three fingers at chest height. Candlelight, cold stone, an enormous dark space above them.

entries.mnemonic: Stand in the middle of a crossroads and you can see four ways at once. Thai calls that place a sìi-yɛ̂ɛk, a four-split, because sìi is four — and it sounds like exactly what you do standing there. (▁ low and flat, a short glance down each road)
entries.headline: Sìi.
entries.scene: Seen from above: a dusty rural crossroads at midday where two straight roads meet, each of the four arms running away to the horizon across parched fields. A lone figure stands dead centre, shading their eyes, turned to look down one of them. Hard black shadows.

entries.mnemonic: Palm up, all five fingers spread, and she slaps it into his hard enough to sting — both of them laughing, hâa! Five fingers and one laugh, and the laugh is the word. Nothing else to remember. (↓ falling, the laugh drops as the hands meet)
entries.headline: Hâa!
entries.scene: Two friends mid high-five on an outdoor basketball court, palms just meeting, both heads tipped back laughing, all five fingers of each hand spread wide and clearly visible. Hair and clothes still in motion. Bright afternoon light, chain-link fence behind them.

entries.mnemonic: Six ham hocks hang from six hooks in the butcher's window, and he counts them off along the rail with the back of his knife. Hock, hòk: the meat and the number are the same short syllable, and both stop dead at the k. (▁ low and blunt, cut off at the end)
entries.headline: hòk.
entries.scene: A butcher's window seen from inside the shop: six cured ham hocks hanging in a row from hooks on a steel rail. A butcher in a striped apron runs the back of a knife along them, lips moving as he counts. Tiled walls, sawdust floor, cold daylight through the glass.

entries.mnemonic: Seven jets tear across the sky in one arrowhead, trailing coloured smoke. Count them off as they pass — jèt — one blunt syllable for each. Seven jets, and jèt is seven. (▁ low and flat, short and hard as a jet going over)
entries.headline: Jèt!
entries.scene: Seven fighter jets in a tight arrowhead formation streaking low across a clear blue sky, coloured smoke trails fanning out behind them. Along the bottom of the frame, a crowd of upturned silhouetted faces and raised hands.

entries.mnemonic: An octopus gets into the cricket bag and comes up with a bat in every arm — eight arms, eight bats, all swinging at once while the fielders back away. BAT gives you bpàaet, and the animal does the counting for you. (▁ low and flat, cut off short by the t)
entries.headline: bpàaet!
entries.scene: An octopus rising out of a cricket bag on a village green with a wooden bat gripped in each of its eight arms, all raised at different angles. Two fielders stumble backwards with their hands up and their caps falling off. Sunny afternoon, white boundary rope, a pavilion in the distance.

entries.mnemonic: The herd files into the milking shed and the farmer counts them through the gate. The ninth cow is always the one that stops in the doorway to think about it, and the gate comes down behind her. Nine cows: gâo. (↓ falling, the gate drops)
entries.headline: gâo.
entries.scene: A milking shed doorway at dusk. Eight cows are already inside the lit shed; the ninth stands square in the open gateway, head turned back, refusing to move. A farmer leans on the gatepost with one hand raised mid-count. Mud, straw, blue evening outside and yellow light within.

entries.mnemonic: Ten small glasses along the counter and one sip from each: by the last of them she has counted the whole row without thinking about it. sìp is ten, and ten sips is the row. (▁ low and flat, short as a single dry sip)
entries.headline: Sìp.
entries.scene: A long cellar counter lined with ten small tasting glasses. Nine stand drained; a sommelier lifts the tenth to her lips, eyes closed, her other hand spread flat on the wood. Oak barrels stacked behind her, warm lamplight.

entries.mnemonic: sìp is ten, and twenty is two tens — but not sǎwng-sìp, as you would expect. Thai keeps an older word for two in this one slot and puts it on the front: yîi-sìp. Two towers of ten coins side by side, one of them noticeably more tarnished than the other. (▁ the second half drops low and short, stopped by the p)
entries.headline: yîi-sìp.
entries.scene: Two neat towers of ten coins each standing side by side on a dark wooden counter, one tower bright and the other badly tarnished, a shopkeeper's hand resting beside them. Low warm light raking across the coins, long shadows behind.

entries.mnemonic: Sun, chart: sǎn-châat. Dawn comes up through the airport hall and the queue holds people dressed for a dozen different countries, every one of them waiting to answer the same question. Which nation are you. That answer is the sǎn-châat. (↑ sǎn climbs, then châat drops flat, like a stamp coming down)
entries.headline: sǎn-châat?
entries.scene: A glass-walled airport hall at sunrise, low orange light stretching across the floor. A long queue of travellers in varied traditional dress — embroidered coats, saris, robes, wool caps — waits at a booth where an officer leans forward with one hand outstretched, palm up. Long shadows, early-morning stillness.

entries.thai: ยินดีต้อนรับ
entries.mnemonic: Two halves, both honest. yin-dii is glad — the same glad you meet in pleased to meet you. dtâawn-ráp, torn and rap, is to receive. Glad to receive you is how Thai says welcome, and the door swings wide on the last syllable. (▲ ráp lifts high as the door swings wide)
entries.headline: Yin-dii dtâawn-ráp!
entries.scene: A wooden Thai house at dusk, its front door thrown wide. The owner stands in the warm light of the hallway with both arms spread and a jasmine garland over one wrist, beaming at three travellers coming up the path with bags on their shoulders.

entries.thai: ด้วยความยินดี
entries.mnemonic: It is with pleasure, word for word. dûuai is with. khwaam-yin-dii is the gladness, and dii, good, sits on the end of it. The porter sets the case down inside the door, straightens up, waves away the offered note and means every syllable. (— the last syllable lands flat and easy, no effort in it)
entries.headline: dûuai khwaam-yin-dii.
entries.scene: A hotel porter who has just set a heavy suitcase down inside a doorway, straightening up with one hand still on the handle and the other waving away a banknote held out by the guest, smiling broadly. Bright lobby, polished floor, morning light through glass doors.

entries.mnemonic: It is the French word for French, slowed down and given a Thai mouth: français becomes fà-ràng-sèet. The middle of it, farang, is also the everyday Thai word for a Westerner, so France comes out as the farang country. (▁ the first two syllables sit low and short)
entries.headline: fà-ràng-sèet.
entries.scene: A pavement café under a wrought-iron balcony on a grey morning in Paris. A man in a beret plays an accordion beside a round marble table set with coffee and croissants; the great iron tower stands hazy at the end of the street. Wet cobbles, bare plane trees.

entries.mnemonic: Take ANGRY and stop it dead with a t: ang-grìt. A bowler-hatted man stands in the rain glaring at a cup of tea gone stone cold, furious and entirely silent about it. That is England. (▁ the second syllable drops low and stops short)
entries.headline: ang-grìt.
entries.scene: A grey wet street. A man in a bowler hat and long dark coat stands under a black umbrella, rain sheeting off it, glaring down at a cup and saucer balanced on a low wall in front of him, his face red with contained fury.

entries.mnemonic: Thai cannot begin a word with sp, so it slips a tiny sa in front and comes out with sa-bpeen: Spain, with a step taken in the doorway first. The heel comes down on the tiles and the guitar answers it. (— bpeen stays flat and level, like the long note held under the stamping)
entries.headline: sà-bpeen.
entries.scene: A sunlit whitewashed courtyard. A flamenco dancer in a red ruffled dress is caught mid-stamp, back arched, one arm curved high above her head; a guitarist sits behind her on a wooden chair, head bent over the strings. Hard shadows, terracotta pots, an old tiled floor.

entries.mnemonic: She sings one last la— down the platform and then she is gone. laa-gɔ̀ɔn: a la, and gone. It is the goodbye for someone leaving properly, not the see-you-tomorrow kind. (▁ gɔ̀ɔn drops low, the sound of a door pulled shut)
entries.headline: Laa-gɔ̀ɔn…
entries.scene: A railway platform at dusk. A woman leans out of the window of a moving carriage with one arm raised in a wave, mouth open mid-note; on the emptying platform a man watches the train shrink away. Steam, low orange sun down the tracks.

entries.mnemonic: Say the first half of ROYAL and stop: rɔ́ɔy. The palace gate swings back and the guard comes out a hundred strong, rank behind rank behind rank, filling the whole courtyard for the sake of one man on a balcony. A hundred is the royal number. (▲ high and taut, pitched up over the drums)
entries.headline: rɔ́ɔy!
entries.scene: A vast palace courtyard at dawn with rank upon rank of ceremonial guards in white and gold standing in perfect grid formation, filling the frame to the far wall. A single small figure on a high balcony looks down on them. Long shadows, pale gold light.

entries.mnemonic: The word is already yours, but English says Thai with a dip in the middle of it and the Thai word does not move at all. Hold it dead level from start to finish. ไท also means free, which is why the country reads as the land of the free. (— perfectly flat; no rise, no drop, no dip)
entries.headline: thai.
entries.scene: A wide rice paddy at dawn, the flooded fields lying mirror-flat to the horizon. A farmer in a straw hat stands upright at the edge of the water, arms loose at his sides, looking level at the far bank where a golden temple spire catches the first light.

entries.mnemonic: The old man's hand sweeps a wide arc: in my day— and he is off, describing a whole era. sà-mǎi is that era, a period, an age. The mǎi on the end climbs exactly like the mǎi that turns a sentence into a question. (↑ rising, the voice lifts as the hand sweeps)
entries.headline: …sà-mǎi.
entries.scene: An old man in a rattan chair on a wooden veranda, one hand raised and sweeping through a wide arc, eyes bright, mouth open mid-story. Four grandchildren sit cross-legged on the boards around him looking up. Late afternoon light through banana leaves.

entries.mnemonic: Three children are digging up the vegetable patch and the noise is tremendous: spades ringing on stone, shrieking, black earth going over the fence. A din. And din is the very stuff they are throwing about, the soil itself. (— flat and level, said as plainly as the ground)
entries.headline: din!
entries.scene: A back garden vegetable patch churned into a crater. Three children with spades fling dark crumbly soil over their shoulders, mouths open in shrieks, earth hanging in the air around them. A dog barks at the edge of the hole. Bright afternoon, washing on a line behind.

entries.mnemonic: A yard full of children raising a din — and a cloud of dirt with it. Every shout brings up more dust; the din and the dirt come off the same ground. din is that earth under their bare feet. (— flat and level, one steady note under the noise)
entries.headline: din.
entries.scene: A bare dusty schoolyard in hard sunlight. Half a dozen barefoot children mid-chase, mouths open shouting, a thick golden cloud of dust boiling up around their feet; their shins and hands caked with dry earth. A wall and a mango tree behind.

entries.mnemonic: Take CLOWN and drop the n: klàao. In the middle of the chaos the clown climbs onto a chair, takes his hat off, holds it over his heart and makes a short and entirely serious speech to the ring. klàao is saying as a formal act — stating a thing aloud. (▁ low and flat, the voice of someone being serious for once)
entries.headline: klàao.
entries.scene: A circus ring. A clown in full paint stands on a wooden chair with his hat held over his heart, mouth open mid-speech, completely solemn. Acrobats and a small elephant have stopped to listen and the crowd in the dark stands beyond is silent. One spotlight, sawdust floor.

entries.mnemonic: Nothing is settled until it is tied down. The old sailor takes the rope, finds the exact spot along it and pulls a hard knot into place. Come and knot it, kam-nòt, and now the date exists. It is the word for fixing a thing to a precise point: a deadline, a price, a rule. (— flat on kam, then nòt drops low as the knot pulls tight)
entries.headline: kam-nòt.
entries.scene: Close view of a weathered sailor's hands hauling a thick rope taut and pulling a knot tight at one point along it, the rest of the rope coiling away across the deck planks. Salt-stained fingers, frayed hemp, hard low sunlight across the wood.

entries.mnemonic: The old carpenter lays his hands over the boy's on the saw and pushes, pulls, pushes, until the plank is sawn through. He does not cut it for him. sǎawn is that: teaching, passing the thing on. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the saw coming back up)
entries.headline: Sǎawn.
entries.scene: A dusty workshop. An old carpenter stands behind a boy at a sawhorse with his weathered hands laid over the boy's on the saw handle, a plank half cut through beneath them, curls of sawdust drifting in a shaft of light from a grimy window.

entries.mnemonic: Take QUALM and drop the m: kʰwǎa. At the fork she gets a qualm about it, hangs there a full second with both hands locked on the wheel — and then swings right anyway. The doubt lives in the sound; the turn is the meaning. (↑ rising, the voice lifts like the question she is asking herself)
entries.headline: kʰwǎa.
entries.scene: A car stopped at a rural fork in the road, seen head on. The driver, hands tense on the wheel, is turned to look down the right-hand branch with a worried frown while the front wheels have just begun to bite that way. Two dusty roads diverge around a lone tree. Flat afternoon light.

entries.mnemonic: Same road, same hour, same jam — your regular jam, every single morning of your life. pràʔ-tɕam is the thing that happens on schedule and is always there: the regular customer, the regular route, the usual. (— tɕam levels out flat, the same every single morning)
entries.headline: pràʔ-tɕam.
entries.scene: An elevated view of a city expressway at sunrise, solid with unmoving cars stretching to the horizon between hazy office towers. A single motorcyclist threads the narrow gap between two lanes. Long shadows, exhaust haze, flat gold light.

entries.mnemonic: A rooster struts down the middle of the lane like he owns it — that guy. gài is chicken, and the cockerel is the guy who runs the yard: the dog steps round him, the hens get out of the way. (▁ low and flat, one short cluck)
entries.headline: Gài!
