entries.scene: A village lane at dawn. An enormous glossy rooster struts down the centre of it, chest thrown out and tail high, while a dog and two hens step aside onto the verge. Wooden houses either side, mist between them, low golden light.

entries.mnemonic: The cockerel owns the yard. Chest out, wings flared, beak up, squaring off against a dog twice his size and winning, while the hens watch from the coop door. Some guy, says the farmer. gài is the bird, GUY is the sound. (▁ low and flat, a short blunt syllable)
entries.headline: gài.
entries.scene: A bantam cockerel in a farmyard standing chest out with wings flared and beak raised, squaring up to a large dog twice his size that is backing away with its ears flat. Hens watch from a coop doorway. Dusty yard, low golden evening light.

entries.mnemonic: A jar of jam is wedged under the door and it is the only thing holding the place open: take it away and everything shuts. เป็น bpen means to be, so jam-bpen is what has to be. Not wanted, not nice. Necessary. (— both syllables flat and level; there is nothing to argue with)
entries.headline: jam-bpen.
entries.scene: A heavy wooden door propped open by a squat jar of dark red jam jammed under its bottom edge, the door leaning its weight onto the glass. Beyond it a busy corridor of people passing through. Low camera angle close to the floor, hard daylight from the corridor.

entries.mnemonic: kìaw is to hook — the curved blade that catches a whole armful of stalks in one pull. kàp is with. Hooked-with is how Thai says about: whatever catches on the subject comes up along with it. (▁ both syllables sit low and flat)
entries.headline: …kìaw-kàp…
entries.scene: Close on a farmer's hands in a paddy field: a curved sickle pulled through a stand of golden rice, a thick armful of stalks caught in the hook and bending with it, chaff flying up. Flooded fields and low hills behind, hard midday sun.

entries.mnemonic: Put a G in front of EARN: gəən. By the tenth of the month the little shop has already earned its whole target, and the takings have gone on past the top of the jar and out over the counter. To go beyond the mark is the word. It rhymes with dəən, walk. (— flat and level, no drama in the going past)
entries.headline: gəən.
entries.scene: A small shop counter with a glass jar so full of banknotes and coins that the lid will not sit down, notes spilling over the rim onto the counter. The shopkeeper stands behind it with both hands raised in astonishment. Shelves of goods behind, warm afternoon light through the window.

entries.mnemonic: Say the end of tyCOON, but with your lips pulled wide in a grin instead of pushed forward, and you land the Thai vowel: kʰɯɯn. The tycoon walks into the little family shop and hands back the keys and the cash box, all of it, with both hands. Returned. (— flat and level, the tone of a thing simply given back)
entries.headline: kʰɯɯn.
entries.scene: A man in an expensive overcoat standing in a cramped family shop, holding out an open cash box and a ring of keys with both hands toward an elderly couple behind the counter. The couple stare, one hand half raised. A large car waits at the kerb beyond the window. Cold daylight outside, warm light within.

entries.mnemonic: Everything in the room is sub-par. Put a p on the end of sub-par and you have sà-pʰâap: the condition a thing is in. Good or bad, it is the state of it — a room's, a car's, a body's after a long week. (↓ pʰâap drops away, like a shoulder sagging at the sight)
entries.headline: sà-pʰâap.
entries.scene: A man stands in the doorway of a small rented room with his arms folded, unimpressed. Peeling ceiling, a stained mattress on a bare frame, a bucket catching a drip, one naked bulb. Grey daylight through a cracked window, dust on the sill.

entries.mnemonic: A whole country's work runs up one long table and into the mouth of a single vast man: farmers, bakers, dockers, all of it passed hand over hand to sate a git. SATE, A, GIT — sèet-thà-gìt, the machine that moves everything somewhere. (▁ low and clipped, the last syllable stopped dead)
entries.headline: sèet-thà-gìt.
entries.scene: A vast banquet hall with an impossibly long table receding into the distance. At the near end an enormously fat man in evening dress is being fed from silver dishes, while along the whole length of the table farmers, bakers and dock workers pass laden platters hand over hand toward him. Chandeliers, deep shadows, soot on the workers' faces.

entries.mnemonic: The same chow as cháaw, morning — but let the voice fall instead of holding it up high and the meaning changes to rent. The morning goes up; the rent comes down, out of your hand and into the landlady's. (↓ falling, the voice drops as the notes leave your fingers)
entries.headline: Châo.
entries.scene: A shophouse doorway at dusk. A young tenant counts banknotes one by one into the open palm of an elderly landlady, who holds a ring of keys in her other hand. His rucksack sits on the step; a narrow staircase rises into the dark behind her.

entries.mnemonic: A free gift, this one: dtaai is very nearly the English word for what it means. An old man sits still in a chair by an open window and his hand falls open on the armrest, and the small bird he was holding lifts away into the light. Say die, but flat — no fall, no rise. (— level and undramatic, which is the strange part of it)
entries.headline: dtaai.
entries.scene: An old man motionless in a high-backed chair beside an open window, his hand fallen open on the armrest. A small bird that had been perched on his fingers is lifting away toward the bright window. Thin curtains moving in the draught, a shaft of pale light across an otherwise empty room.

entries.mnemonic: One tent pole juts out of line and the whole camp is chaos. The Khan rides down the row pointing with his crop — pole in, fire out, wagons straight — and in five minutes it is dealt with. Jut, then Khan: jàt-gaan, taking a mess and handling it. (— the second syllable runs out flat and long, the calm afterwards)
entries.headline: jàt-gaan.
entries.scene: A steppe encampment of round felt tents in disarray, one pole leaning badly out of the line. A commander on horseback rides down the row pointing with a riding crop while people scramble to straighten ropes and stamp out a fire. Dust, wide grassland, low sun.

entries.mnemonic: โรง is the building — the same โรง that sits in cinema, hotel and factory — and เรียน is to learn. Put the hall and the learning together and school falls out of it: roong-riian, the learning hall. Take โรง away with you; it builds half a town. (— both syllables level and even, like a held bell)
entries.headline: roong-riian.
entries.scene: A school courtyard at morning assembly. Rows of children in white shirts and navy shorts stand in the dust facing a long low building with an open verandah, hands at their sides. A teacher stands at the front with one arm raised. The shadow of a flagpole, green trees, early sun.

entries.mnemonic: Allow me, says the old man, and he is away into a story that lasts an hour. The low sitting inside allow is lâw: to tell, to narrate, to spin the whole thing out while everyone leans in closer. (↓ falling, the voice drops as he settles into it)
entries.headline: Lâw…
entries.scene: Night. A village elder sits on a low stool beside a cooking fire, hands mid-gesture shaping something large in the air, mouth open in speech. A ring of children and adults sit close around him, faces lit orange, leaning in. Dark trees beyond.

entries.mnemonic: Ma hands the child a nut and a rounded stone and guides her hands to show her how. Nothing else in that forest is doing anything of the kind. Ma, nut — má-nút, the one creature that makes a tool out of the world it finds. (▲ both syllables up high and taut, bright as the shell cracking)
entries.headline: má-nút.
entries.scene: A mother crouched on a forest floor guiding her small daughter's hands, which hold a rounded stone above a hard nut set on a flat rock. Both are wholly absorbed. Dappled green light through a high canopy, monkeys watching from a branch above them.

entries.mnemonic: Tick, and on the tock the coconut lets go. It is a hand's width above the dust now, directly over a man who has slept through the whole business. ตก is anything that falls: rain, prices, a man off a ladder. (▁ low and short, the sound of the landing)
entries.headline: tòk.
entries.scene: Beneath a coconut palm at noon. A large green coconut hangs frozen in the air a hand's width above the dusty ground, right beside a man dozing against the trunk with his hat over his face. A cat is already leaping clear. Hard light, sharp shadows.

entries.mnemonic: The knitter will not start until the wool is sorted — each kind in its own basket, thick with thick, red with red, no mixing. chá-nít is exactly that: the sort, the type, which kind of thing you are holding. (▲ both syllables high and quick, the snap of a decision)
entries.headline: chá-nít.
entries.scene: An old woman on a wooden veranda surrounded by six open baskets, each holding balls of wool of a different colour and thickness. She is placing one ball deliberately into its matching basket, knitting needles tucked under her arm. Soft afternoon light.

entries.mnemonic: On the bus the barrister balances his case across one raised knee and carries it that way the whole journey, arms folded over the top of it, letting nobody near. Carry, knee: kà-rá-nii, the case in question. (— the last syllable lands flat and is held the longest)
entries.headline: kà-rá-nii.
entries.scene: A barrister in a dark suit sitting on a crowded bus with a battered leather briefcase balanced across one raised knee, arms folded protectively over it, staring out of a rain-streaked window. Other passengers pressed in around him. Grey morning light, condensation on the glass.

entries.mnemonic: The road-mender wipes his forehead with a tarry glove and leaves a perfect black ring round one eye. Everybody who passes looks at that eye and at nothing else on him. dtaa is the eye, and the tar has drawn a circle round it. (— flat and level, an unblinking stare)
entries.headline: dtaa.
entries.scene: Close portrait of a road worker in a high-visibility vest staring straight at the viewer, one eye ringed with a smear of glossy black tar, the glove that did it still raised near his temple. Behind him a steaming tar barrel and a torn-up road. Flat overcast light.

entries.mnemonic: dtaa is the eye. It is also your mother's father — the old man on the porch whose eye is on you the whole afternoon. One flat syllable, the same one you say as a casual ta, does both jobs: the watcher and the watching. (— flat and level, an unhurried old voice)
entries.headline: Dtaa.
entries.scene: Close portrait of an elderly Thai man seated on a wooden porch, deeply lined face, both hands resting on a walking stick, watching steadily with clear attentive eyes. Beyond him, softly out of focus, a small child plays in a green sunlit yard.

entries.mnemonic: A pat of butter running into a warm split bun, and a mouth halfway through the first chew. Not the bun from yesterday, not tomorrow's — this one, in your mouth, now. Pat, chew, bun: pàt-tɕù-ban, the present moment and nothing either side of it. (— the last syllable settles flat, right where you are)
entries.headline: pàt-tɕù-ban.
entries.scene: A close view of a person mid-bite into a warm split bun, a yellow pat of butter melting and running at the edge, crumbs on their lip, eyes closed in concentration. A kitchen table, a knife laid down, steam still rising from the cut face of the bun. Soft morning light.

entries.mnemonic: The cook sighs, then tips one more fistful of chilli into the wok anyway. sài is that: to put something in, or on — the chilli into the pot, the shirt onto your back, the sugar into the cup. (▁ low, the sound of a long breath going out)
entries.headline: sài.
entries.scene: Close on a blackened wok over a flame, a cook's hand tipping a fistful of dried red chillies into it. Steam and smoke rise into her face; her eyes are half closed and her cheeks puffed as she breathes out. Night market stall lights behind.

entries.mnemonic: The thing in the back yard has not moved in years: rot in the sills, rot through the floor, moss on the roof and a young tree grown straight up through the bonnet. rót is any vehicle at all, and this one is going nowhere ever again. (▲ high and taut, cut off short and hard)
entries.headline: rót.
entries.scene: A rusted-out car sitting on flat tyres in a weed-choked back yard, its bonnet buckled by a young tree that has grown up through it, moss thick on the roof, one door hanging open on a broken hinge. Grass up to the wheel arches. Grey overcast light.

entries.mnemonic: A phone lies face down in a puddle in the middle of the road, ringing and ringing while the rain hammers it flat, and nobody is coming for it. fǒn is that rain, and the voice climbs the way a ring tone does. (↑ rising, the pitch lifts like a phone waiting to be answered)
entries.headline: fǒn.
entries.scene: A tarmac road in a downpour, seen low and close. A mobile phone lies face down in a shallow puddle, rain bouncing off its back in bright crowns. The street beyond dissolves into grey water and blurred headlights. Everything soaked, nobody in sight.

entries.mnemonic: The cart sits tilted in the road with one wheel gone entirely, its axle down in the dirt and fruit spilled everywhere. kʰàat is what is wrong with it: short of something, missing a piece, not complete. (▁ low and flat, stopped short)
entries.headline: kʰàat.
entries.scene: A wooden handcart tipped at a steep angle in a dusty lane, one wheel missing altogether and its bare axle resting in the dirt, oranges spilled across the ground. An old vendor stands with hands on hips staring at the empty axle. Hot midday light.

entries.mnemonic: Split a length of bamboo and the hollow core is cut across at intervals by hard pale rings — the joints, the places where it is divided into separate sections. Say CORE the British way with no r on the end and you have kʰɔ̂ɔ. (↓ falling, dropping onto each hard ring in turn)
entries.headline: kʰɔ̂ɔ.
entries.scene: A length of thick green bamboo split lengthways on a workbench, its hollow interior divided at intervals by pale hard rings. A craftsman's thumb rests on one of the rings. Shavings across the bench, warm workshop light through a dusty window.

entries.mnemonic: A rat is sitting up in the great carved chair at the head of the marble chamber, and the ministers file in and bow to it anyway. Wherever the power happens to be sitting, that is the rát: the state. (▲ high and taut, the way a title is announced)
entries.headline: rát.
entries.scene: A marble parliamentary chamber with columns and tiered benches. A large brown rat sits upright in the ornate carved chair on the raised dais, tail curled over the armrest. Two rows of officials in dark suits bow toward it, heads down. Shafts of dusty light from high windows.

entries.mnemonic: People press gold leaf onto the great city pillar and ask it for luck. làk is the pillar itself — and from there, anything central: the main thing, the principle that everything else is built around. (▁ low and short, solid as the stone)
entries.headline: làk.
entries.scene: A gilded stone pillar inside a shrine, heaped with marigold garlands at its base. A kneeling woman presses a square of gold leaf onto it with her thumb; incense smoke drifts across and other worshippers blur behind her in the warm dim light.

entries.mnemonic: Some red: the ribbon across the finish line. She takes it on the chest and it snaps and streams back off both shoulders, her arms already up. sǎm-rèt is that exact moment, the thing finished, the thing achieved. Clip the end of red short and the Thai is there. (↑ sǎm climbs, then rèt sits low and clipped as the ribbon breaks)
entries.headline: sǎm-rèt.
entries.scene: A runner breaking a broad red ribbon at a finish line, the ribbon torn and streaming back from her shoulders, both arms flung up, mouth open in a shout. Blurred crowd behind the barriers, other runners far back down the track. Bright hard stadium daylight.

entries.mnemonic: kʰwaam- is the noun-maker again, the qualm sound on the front; jing is true. Strike a cracked bell and it thuds — strike a true one and it rings out clean, jing. kʰwaam-jing is the truth itself, the thing that rings. (— both syllables flat and level, no argument in it)
entries.headline: kʰwaam-jing.
entries.scene: A hand swings a padded wooden mallet against a great hanging bronze bell in a temple courtyard. The bell shivers with the strike and a dozen birds burst off the eaves above it. Clear morning light, swept stone, saffron robes blurred behind.

entries.mnemonic: Hidden inside sàp-daa is the same ancient seven that sits inside September — sapta, seven, carried along by both languages since long before either met the other. A week is seven days: seven small lamps in a row along a sill, six of them lit and a hand bringing the taper to the last. (— the second syllable runs out long and flat)
entries.headline: sàp-daa.
entries.scene: A row of seven small oil lamps along a stone windowsill, the first six burning and the seventh being lit by a hand holding a taper. Deep blue dusk beyond the window, warm pools of light on the stone, nothing else in the frame.

entries.mnemonic: Four men are hammering at a coconut and getting nowhere. The cook walks over, turns it in her palm and opens it with one tap of the cleaver's spine. That is the witty way: wí-thii, the method. A hard t in the middle, never an English th. (— the second syllable holds flat and long, wi-THEE)
entries.headline: wí-thii.
entries.scene: An outdoor kitchen. Four men crouch over a coconut with hammers and a rock, husk fibres scattered everywhere. Beside them a small woman in an apron holds a coconut in one palm, the spine of her cleaver tapping its middle, the shell already opening cleanly in two. Amused glances, dappled shade.

entries.mnemonic: Say the first half of CHUTNEY and stop: tɕʰút. He is two steps out of the door in the new outfit, pressed and immaculate, when the spoon tips and a gout of chutney lands down the whole front of it. The outfit was the point, and the outfit is finished. (▲ high and taut, the yelp he does not manage to swallow)
entries.headline: tɕʰút!
entries.scene: A young man frozen in a hallway doorway in a crisp new suit, arms held out from his sides, a bright orange-brown splatter of chutney down the front of his jacket. A tipped spoon still in one hand, a bowl on the hall table beside him. Harsh hallway light, his face aghast.

entries.mnemonic: At dawn a woman kneels and spoons rice into a monk's bowl, and he will thaan it. Where kin is blunt and everyday, thaan is the soft, polite word for eat — the one you use for a guest, an elder, a monk. (— flat and level, gently said)
entries.headline: thaan.
entries.scene: Dawn on a Thai street. A woman kneels barefoot on the pavement spooning rice into the alms bowl of a monk in saffron robes, his eyes lowered and head bowed; a line of monks waits behind him in the mist. Soft pink light, shuttered shopfronts.

entries.mnemonic: Someone holds a mug out to the sentry on the gate and he does not even turn his head: nah — not while he is on. NAH plus TEA gives nâa-thîi, the thing that is yours to do whether you fancy it or not, and whether the tea is going cold or not. (↓ both halves drop, firm and final)
entries.headline: Nâa-thîi.
entries.scene: A uniformed sentry standing rigid at a gatehouse in the rain, eyes fixed straight ahead, while a colleague beside him holds out a steaming enamel mug. The sentry has not moved at all. Water running off the peak of his cap, wet cobbles, grey dawn light.

entries.mnemonic: Am-purr. Every cat owns a district: the wall, the three roofs and the alley it patrols twice a night, and it sits on the boundary at dusk to look the whole of it over. An amphoe is exactly that, the patch of country belonging to one office. (— both syllables flat and level, like the purr itself)
entries.headline: am-pʰəə.
entries.scene: A large cat sitting upright on a garden wall at dusk, tail curled round its feet, surveying a sprawl of tiled rooftops, alleys and treetops below. Lights are coming on in the houses. Its eyes are half closed and entirely proprietorial. Warm dusk, deep blue sky.

entries.mnemonic: Two pieces, and you have one of them already: dəən is the walk, thaang is the way or road. Walk plus way is how a man gets to work — the same wet pavement, the same hour, every morning of his life, in a river of other people doing exactly the same. (— both halves flat and level, the same every day)
entries.headline: dəən-thaang.
entries.scene: A man in a raincoat walking a wet city pavement in a stream of other commuters all heading the same direction, umbrellas overlapping, a bus pulling away from the kerb beside them. Shopfront light on the wet paving. Dark early morning, every face turned the same way.

entries.mnemonic: เดิน is to walk, and it starts like earn with a d pushed in front of it; ทาง is the way, the road. Walk the way and you are travelling: dooen-thaang. The word is not about arriving anywhere, it is the going itself. (— both syllables flat and even, like a steady pace)
entries.headline: dooen-thaang.
entries.scene: A traveller with a heavy pack walking away from the viewer up a red dirt road that winds into green hills. Mist still lies in the valley to the left, the sun is just clearing the ridge, and a dog trots along at the traveller's heel. Long morning shadows.

entries.mnemonic: A tour goes everywhere: every street, every corner, every last village on the map, with nothing at all left out. tʰûa is exactly that — throughout, all over, the entire lot of it, the whole country or the whole body. One word for the lot. (↓ falling, the voice sweeps down over the whole view)
entries.headline: tʰûa.
entries.scene: A traveller stands on a hilltop seen from behind with both arms spread wide, looking out over an entire valley of villages, winding roads and paddy fields that runs away in every direction to the hazy horizon. Morning mist, sun breaking through cloud.

entries.mnemonic: That boy is in the muck again. Not once, not as a treat — always, every single day, straight off the dry path and into the deepest part of it, up to the elbows. mák is the word for the thing somebody is forever doing. (▲ high and taut, cut off by the k, said through the teeth)
entries.headline: mák.
entries.scene: A small boy standing knee-deep in a brown farmyard puddle, grinning, arms spread wide, mud to his elbows and across his face. On the dry path a woman waits with a towel over her arm and no surprise at all on her face. Wellington boots by a gate, grey drizzle, farm buildings behind.

entries.mnemonic: A full tum, Ma in one chair, Da in the other, and absolutely nothing happening. No visitors, no news, the same supper as last week and the cat asleep in the same spot on the rug. tham-má-daa is a Tuesday: plain, normal, exactly as it always is. (— the last syllable runs out flat and even, the tone of nothing much)
entries.headline: tham-má-daa.
entries.scene: A small living room in the evening. An older couple sit in two armchairs, one dozing with hands folded over a full stomach, the other slowly stirring a cup. A cat asleep on the rug, a cleared supper table behind them. Ordinary lamp light, curtains drawn, nothing remarkable anywhere in the room.

entries.mnemonic: At the end of the line the robot arm swings a box down and stacks it onto a wooden pallet, thump, and the pallet fills and another comes up empty behind it. pà-lìt is the making itself: what a factory does all day, every day. (▁ low and flat, the thump of the pallet taking the weight)
entries.headline: pà-lìt.
entries.scene: A factory floor at the end of an assembly line. A yellow robot arm lowers a plain sealed box onto a wooden pallet already stacked shoulder-high with identical boxes; a forklift waits to one side with its forks raised. Overhead strip lighting, polished concrete, conveyor rollers.

entries.mnemonic: The shoe has given up at the front and his big toe is straight out through the end of it. He has grown again, in a month, and the next pair will go the same way. TOE gives you toː: getting big, and the growing that does it. (— flat and level, steady as growth itself)
entries.headline: toː.
entries.scene: A close low view of a child's scuffed school shoe with the big toe pushed right through a split across the front, the foot planted on a doorstep. Blurred above and behind, a parent's hands hold a pencil flat against a doorframe already marked with faint height lines.

entries.mnemonic: พ่อ is PAW, the father, with a round aw in the middle. พา is PAH, with an open ah, and it means to take someone along with you. Here the pa does both: his hand closes round the child's wrist and he tows her through the crowd without breaking stride. (— flat and level, the pace never changes)
entries.headline: pʰaa.
entries.scene: A packed night market seen from behind. A tall father in a work shirt cuts through the crowd with a small girl's wrist held firmly in his hand, her feet skipping to keep up, her free hand clutching a skewer. Steam, hanging bulbs, shoulders and elbows all around.

entries.mnemonic: jɔɔm is to give in; ráp is to receive. Give in and take it, and you have accepted. There is a rap at the door, and you can either leave it knocking or open up and receive whatever is standing out there. (▲ ráp snaps up high, the moment of taking it)
entries.headline: …ráp.
entries.scene: A man stands in his open front doorway at night, one hand still on the latch, taking a heavy wrapped parcel from a courier standing in the rain. His shoulders are dropped and his expression resigned but steady. Hall light spills onto wet steps.

entries.mnemonic: This is a cousin of the English word rather than a coincidence: sà-thǎa-nii and station both come down from an old root meaning to stand. A place where things stand still a while — the train breathing at the platform, everybody waiting, nothing moving yet. (— the last syllable runs out flat and long, held like the wait)
entries.headline: sà-thǎa-nii.
entries.scene: A train standing at a platform with heat shimmer around its wheels and its doors open, a scattering of passengers with bags waiting along the platform edge, one of them leaning out to look up the track. High iron-and-glass roof, dusty shafts of light.

entries.mnemonic: tàt is cut and jai is heart, and the sǐn between them sounds like sin. To decide, in Thai, is to cut the sin out of your heart: end the dithering, choose the path, go. (↑ sǐn climbs in the middle, then jai lands flat and final)
entries.headline: Dtàt-sǐn-jai!
entries.scene: A woman stands at a fork in a forest path at dusk, pack already shouldered, one hand pressed flat over her heart and the other making a single decisive chopping motion in the air. Her body is turned toward the left-hand path. Mist between dark trees.

entries.mnemonic: Say AROMA and stop before the last vowel: aa-rom. Bread comes out of the oven and fills the house, and the man who came in slamming doors drops his bag, shuts his eyes and softens where he stands. The smell changed the mood, and the word is the mood. (— both syllables flat and even, settling)
entries.headline: aa-rom.
entries.scene: A kitchen doorway. A man still in his coat stands with his bag dropped at his feet and his shoulders come down, eyes half closed, facing a tray of loaves just lifted from the oven by someone else in the room. Steam rising off the bread. Warm oven light spilling into a dim hallway.

entries.mnemonic: ผู้ is the one-who, the same ผู้ that starts the words for man and woman, and ใหญ่ is big. An adult is simply the big one: the person who takes the jar off the top shelf without going up on anything. phûu-yài. (↓ phûu drops, then yài settles low, with the weight of being the big one)
entries.headline: phûu-yài.
entries.scene: A kitchen. A small girl up on tiptoe on a stool strains toward a plain jar on the highest shelf, fingers short of it by a foot. Beside her a tall woman lifts the same jar down one-handed without stretching, looking somewhere else entirely. Warm afternoon light, tiled wall, open cupboard.

entries.mnemonic: Knock the s off NURSE and you have the end of sà-nɤ̌ɤ. The theatre nurse holds the tray out flat, the instrument laid on it handle first, waiting for the surgeon to take it. That is what sà-nɤ̌ɤ does with an idea: puts it forward. (↑ rising, the voice lifts as the tray comes up)
entries.headline: sà-nɤ̌ɤ.
entries.scene: An operating theatre under a bright overhead lamp. A masked nurse in a green gown extends a steel tray toward a surgeon with both hands, a single clamp laid on it turned handle first. Everything beyond the lamp's circle falls into shadow.

entries.mnemonic: A crow has taken the roof of a parked car for its own: one glossy black bird planted dead centre, turning a single eye on the owner and refusing to shift for him or anybody. Say CAR the British way, with no r on the end, and you have kaa. (— flat and level, one unbothered note)
entries.headline: kaa.
entries.scene: A large glossy black crow standing dead centre on the roof of a dusty parked car, head turned to fix the viewer with one eye, wings slightly open. A man beside the driver's door waves an arm at it without the least effect. Quiet suburban street, hard morning light.

entries.mnemonic: Batting practice in the cage: he pats a ball onto the tee, squares up, bats it away, and then does the whole thing again, and again, two hundred times before the light goes. Pat, tee, bat — pà-tì-bàt, doing a thing over and over until the body owns it. (▁ low and clipped, the flat crack of the bat)
entries.headline: pà-tì-bàt.
entries.scene: A batting cage at dusk. A young player in a helmet places a ball onto a rubber tee with one hand, bat resting on his shoulder, a dozen balls already scattered in the netting behind him. Floodlight glare, dust hanging in the air, a coach watching with folded arms.

entries.mnemonic: A geologist lifts a long core out of the ground under an enormous moon, and everything about the place is there in its bands. kʰɔ̂ɔ is a single item, muun is the raw stuff: core and moon together, kʰɔ̂ɔ-muun, the information. (↓ falls on kʰɔ̂ɔ, then muun levels out flat)
entries.headline: kʰɔ̂ɔ-muun.
entries.scene: Night in an open field. A geologist crouches holding up a long cylindrical soil core banded in coloured layers, turning it in gloved hands under the beam of a head torch. An enormous full moon sits low on the horizon; equipment cases lie open on the grass.

entries.mnemonic: gaan is the piece that turns a doing into a thing — the -ing of it. Put it in front of sùek-sǎa, to study, and you have the whole business: a room of small heads craning at a teacher holding up a jar with something growing in it, hands going up everywhere. (↑ the final syllable climbs, the lift of a question being answered)
entries.headline: gaan-sùek-sǎa.
entries.scene: A classroom of young children at wooden desks, all leaning forward to watch a teacher hold up a glass jar with a plant growing inside it. Hands are raised all over the room. Late afternoon sun through tall windows, dust hanging in the light.
